summary: For 5–7 year olds: rainforests teem with minibeasts, and insects are by far the most numerous animals there. Learners name several rainforest minibeasts, learn a memorable wonder-fact (leaf-cutter ants FARM fungus rather than eat the leaves they carry), notice camouflage (stick insects), and grasp that tiny-but-countless insects vastly outnumber big famous animals like jaguars and monkeys. A gentle insect/not-insect boundary (6 legs = insect; spiders have 8) is reused lightly. The core gallery builds recognition and abundance; a trail/spot game can make a behaviour feel concrete; recall checks follow.
misconceptions: Big animals are the most numerous in the rainforest — insects far outnumber everything else
Leaf-cutter ants eat the leaves they carry — they use them to grow fungus, which they eat
Spiders are insects — they are minibeasts with 8 legs, not 6-legged insects
Stick insects are just twigs — they are living insects camouflaged as twigs
Rainforest insects are all dangerous — most are harmless and vital to the forest

activities.title: Minibeast gallery and the ant-farm wonder-fact
steps: Explore a close-up scene of the forest floor and tree trunks alive with tiny life, and point to or tap each minibeast to learn its name and a hook: jewel/morpho butterfly (colour), giant beetle (size), big spider (size), stick insect (hides), leaf-cutter ants (farmers).

Follow a line of leaf-cutter ants carrying green leaf pieces, then open a drill-down to their underground fungus garden and say in your own words: 'They don't eat the leaves — they grow food (fungus) on them, like farmers.'
Find the twig that is secretly a stick insect (it wiggles when tapped) and explain it is a living insect camouflaged as a twig, not just a stick.
Say gently why the big spider is a minibeast but NOT an insect: count 8 legs (insects have 6).
activities.insight: Rainforests hold a huge variety of minibeasts, and some do surprising things — leaf-cutter ants grow their own food on cut leaves rather than eating them.

activities.title: Which is there most of? Tiny but countless
steps: Answer the question 'Which animals are there MOST of here — big animals like jaguars and monkeys, or tiny insects like ants and beetles?' and lift a flap / reveal to see a swarm answer: insects, by far.
Say why: you see insects everywhere in huge numbers (whole armies of ants), even though each one is tiny, while you rarely see a single jaguar.
Compare an ant trail (many, many ants) with how seldom a jaguar appears, to feel the difference in numbers.
Optional extension: talk about why tiny insects can live in so many more places than one big jaguar (they are small, so many of them fit and find food almost everywhere).
activities.insight: Insects and other minibeasts are by far the most numerous animals in the rainforest — small but countless — far outnumbering the big famous animals.

activities.title: Guide the trail / spot the hidden insect (behaviour mini-game)
steps: Guide the leaf-cutter ant trail to carry leaf pieces home to the fungus garden, narrating what the ants are doing.
Spot the camouflaged stick insect hidden among twigs, then say how its shape and colour help it hide.
activities.insight: Acting out a behaviour or survival trick can help it feel more concrete — carrying leaves to a farm, or finding an animal that hides by looking like its surroundings.

activities.title: Name it and sort it (recall check)
steps: Name a rainforest insect or minibeast and one interesting thing it does.
Sort a few minibeasts into 'insect (6 legs)' and 'not an insect (e.g. spider, 8 legs)'.
Answer: leaf-cutter ants carry bits of leaf back home — what do they use them for?
activities.insight: Secure recall of at least three rainforest minibeasts, the ant-farming behaviour, and the 6-vs-8-leg boundary.

checkQuestion: In a rainforest, are there more big animals like jaguars and monkeys, or more tiny insects like ants and beetles? Which is there more of, and how do you know?
checkAnswer: There are far, far more insects — insects and other minibeasts are the most numerous animals in the rainforest, way more than the big animals. You can tell because they're everywhere in huge numbers (like whole armies of leaf-cutter ants), even though each one is tiny.
